learn.hook: The socket in your room does not give a steady push. Its voltage swings from +311 V to -311 V and back fifty times every second.
points: Alternating voltage varies sinusoidally with time: v = vm sin ωt, where vm is the peak value and ω = 2πν. Most power supplies in homes and industry are AC.
AC is preferred because transformers can easily step its voltage up or down, which makes long-distance transmission efficient.
Across a resistor R, i = (vm/R) sin ωt = im sin ωt: the current is in phase with the voltage.
Over a full cycle, the average current is zero (equal positive and negative halves), but the power i²R is always positive, so the average power is not zero.
Average power in a resistor: P = ½im²R, because the average of sin²ωt over a cycle is ½.

learn.hook: Put an inductor on AC and something strange happens: the current always reaches its peak a quarter cycle after the voltage. The coil makes the current lag.
points: For v = vm sin ωt across inductance L: i = im sin(ωt - π/2). The current lags the voltage by π/2 (90°).
Inductive reactance XL = ωL = 2πνL, unit ohm. Peak current im = vm/XL, and RMS I = V/XL.
XL increases with frequency: an inductor lets DC (ω = 0) pass freely but opposes high-frequency AC.
Average power over a cycle in a pure inductor is zero: energy is stored in its field in one quarter cycle and returned in the next.
The opposition comes from the back emf L di/dt, not from any resistance.

learn.hook: Radio sets, induction furnaces and the power-factor panels in Indian factories all contain resistors, inductors and capacitors in series. Phasors make them easy.
points: In series, the same current flows through R, L and C. VR is in phase with I, VL leads I by 90°, VC lags I by 90°.
Phasor sum: Vm² = VRm² + (VCm - VLm)², so the impedance is Z = √(R² + (XC - XL)²), with vm = imZ.
Impedance diagram: R along one axis and (XC - XL) at right angles; Z is the hypotenuse.
Phase angle: tanφ = (XC - XL)/R. If XL > XC the circuit is inductive (current lags); if XC > XL it is capacitive (current leads).
Individual voltages VR = IR, VL = IXL, VC = IXC can be larger than the supply voltage, because they are not in phase.

topics.title: Power in AC circuits and power factor

learn.hook: Electricity boards in India charge factories a penalty if their power factor is low. A bank of capacitors can save lakhs of rupees a year.
points: Average power in an AC circuit: P = VI cosφ (V and I are RMS), where φ is the phase difference. cosφ is the power factor.
Pure resistor: φ = 0, cosφ = 1, P = VI. Pure inductor or capacitor: φ = ±90°, cosφ = 0, P = 0. Such current is called wattless current.
Series LCR: cosφ = R/Z. At resonance Z = R, so cosφ = 1 and power is maximum.
A low power factor means a large current for the same useful power, so I²R losses in the lines rise.
Industries add capacitors to cancel the lagging current drawn by motors (inductive loads), raising the power factor towards 1.

learn.reallife: State electricity boards, from Maharashtra's MSEDCL to Tamil Nadu's TANGEDCO, set minimum power factor rules for industrial consumers, which is why factories install capacitor banks.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My circuit has current and voltage, so why is the power sometimes zero?'
teach.praise: Chirp! P = VI cosφ, so with a 90° phase difference (pure L or C) the power is zero. Wattless current!
teach.nudge: Good! Which factor in P = VI cosφ can make the power zero?

revise.summary: Average AC power is P = VI cosφ, with cosφ the power factor (R/Z in series LCR). It is 1 for a resistor and at resonance, and 0 for pure L or C (wattless current); capacitors raise low power factors in industry.
focus: Wattless current and power factor correction
traps: A low power factor does not save current; it needs more current for the same power
Don't use peak values in P = VI cosφ; use RMS values

learn.hook: A phone charger steps 230 V down to about 5 V. The power station steps it up to 400 kV. Both use the same simple device: two coils and an iron core.
points: Principle: mutual induction. An alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing flux in a soft iron core, which induces an emf in the secondary coil.
Ideal transformer: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, and with no losses VpIp = VsIs, so Ip/Is = Ns/Np.
Step-up transformer: Ns > Np (voltage raised, current lowered). Step-down transformer: Ns < Np.

Energy losses: flux leakage (reduced by winding coils on top of each other), resistance of windings (thick copper wire), eddy currents in the core (laminated core) and hysteresis (soft iron with a narrow loop).
A transformer works only with AC (or changing current); steady DC gives no changing flux.

example.q: A step-down transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. With 220 V on the primary, find Vs. If the secondary delivers 10 A, find Ip (ideal).

learn.reallife: The grey transformer on an electric pole in an Indian neighbourhood steps 11 kV down to about 415 V between phases (three-phase), which gives about 230-240 V between a phase and neutral for each home.

Thin insulated laminations break these paths

quiz.explain: Steady DC gives no changing flux, so no emf is induced.
steps: Steady DC gives a constant flux in the core
No change of flux ⇒ no induced emf (except at switch-on)
Answer: zero, after the switch-on moment

The principle on which a transformer works is
quiz.explain: The changing flux from the primary induces an emf in the secondary.
steps: Changing current in the primary changes the core flux
This induces emf in the secondary: mutual induction

quiz.q: In a step-up transformer, compared with the primary, the secondary has
options: more turns, higher voltage and lower current
quiz.explain: Power is (ideally) conserved, so raising V lowers I.
steps: Answer: more turns, higher voltage and lower current
quiz.mistake: Thinks both voltage and current step up

quiz.q: A transformer takes 100 W from the supply and delivers 90 W. What is its efficiency (in %)?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can two coils that are not even connected change 230 V into 5 V?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The primary's alternating current makes a changing flux in the core, which induces a voltage in the secondary set by the turns ratio. Wow!
teach.nudge: Good! What links the two coils, and what decides the output voltage?

revise.summary: A transformer works by mutual induction: AC in the primary changes the core flux and induces emf in the secondary. Ideally Vs/Vp = Ns/Np and VpIp = VsIs; losses come from flux leakage, winding resistance, eddy currents and hysteresis.
traps: A step-up transformer does not raise the current; it raises voltage and lowers current
A transformer gives no steady output on DC

topics.title: Power transmission and AC problem solving

learn.hook: Electricity from a hydro plant in Himachal reaches homes in Delhi hundreds of kilometres away. Transformers at both ends make that journey efficient.
points: Power is generated at about 11 to 25 kV, stepped up to hundreds of kV for long-distance lines, then stepped down at substations (to 33 kV, 11 kV and finally 230 V).
For a fixed power P = VI, raising V lowers I, and the line loss I²R falls as 1/V².
Problem example: an ideal step-up transformer from 11 kV to 220 kV has Ns/Np = 20; the line current is 1/20 of the generator current.
Toolkit: V = vm/√2; XL = ωL; XC = 1/(ωC); Z = √(R² + (XC - XL)²); ω₀ = 1/√(LC); P = VI cosφ; Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
Always check whether values given are peak or RMS before using them in formulas.

example.q: A plant generates 800 kW at 4 kV. It is stepped up to 40 kV for a line of resistance 10 Ω. Find the line current and loss.

learn.reallife: POWERGRID's national grid links regional grids through 400 kV and 765 kV AC lines and HVDC links, carrying power from coal belts in the east to cities in the west and north.

Why is the voltage stepped down in several stages (220 kV to 33 kV to 11 kV to 230 V) rather than at once?
options: Transformers cannot step down more than twice
Each stage suits the distance and load of that part of the network, keeping currents and losses manageable
quiz.explain: Higher voltages suit long trunk lines; lower ones suit local distribution safely.
steps: Long trunk lines need very high voltage to keep current low
Local lines and homes need safer lower voltages; each stage suits its part

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does the grid send power at lakhs of volts and then step it down?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Stepping up makes the current small so I²R loss is tiny, then transformers step it down for safe use at home. Smart grid!
teach.nudge: Good! What does raising the voltage do to the current in the lines?

revise.summary: Power is generated at 11–25 kV, stepped up to hundreds of kV for long lines and stepped down in stages to 230 V. For fixed power, higher voltage means lower current and I²R loss falling as 1/V².
traps: Don't mix peak and RMS values; check which is given
Raising V 10 times does not cut the loss only 10 times; it cuts it 100 times
